cues.text: A Childhood of Suffering
Born on 22 July 1647 at Lhautecour in Burgundy, Margaret Mary Alacoque showed an intense devotion to the Blessed Sacrament from early childhood.
Her family's security collapsed after her father's death when she was about eight, leaving the household at the mercy of relatives who treated her and her mother with considerable unkindness.
Around this same period, Margaret was struck by rheumatic fever and resulting paralysis, confining her to bed for four years.
She and her family believed the affliction lifted only after she vowed to the Blessed Virgin to consecrate her life to religious service should she recover.
Her family's later hardships, and her own long convalescence, gave the young Margaret an early, formative acquaintance with suffering she would carry into religious life.
Entering the Visitation
In 1671, Margaret entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial and professed final vows the following year.
This occurred despite a delicate constitution and trials her superiors imposed to test her vocation’s genuineness.
The fairly ordinary formation process gave little outward hint of the extraordinary interior life already unfolding within her.
Visions of the Sacred Heart
Beginning around 1673, Margaret reported a series of profound mystical encounters with Christ.
He, she said, revealed his own Sacred Heart to her, wounded by humanity’s ingratitude and indifference.
He asked that a specific devotion of reparation and love be established in its honor.
This included regular Communion on the first Friday of each month and an hour of prayerful vigil each Thursday night, in memory of his agony in Gethsemane.
Doubted by Her Own Community
These extraordinary claims drew, unsurprisingly, considerable skepticism and even open mockery from within Margaret's own religious community.
Many regarded her reported visions with real suspicion rather than immediate acceptance.

This difficult, often painful period of internal opposition, Margaret bore, by every surviving account, with remarkable patience, understanding that only time and careful examination could establish whether her experiences were genuine.
Vindication Through Patient Scrutiny
Vindication, when it came, arrived slowly and only through the most careful theological examination the Church could apply.
It was not until 1765, seventy-five years after Margaret's death, that Pope Clement XIII formally approved devotion to the Sacred Heart for the wider Church.
Margaret herself was not canonized until 1920—a deliberate, unhurried process reflecting the seriousness with which the Church weighs claims of private revelation before ever endorsing them.
Legacy
Margaret Mary died at Paray-le-Monial on 17 October 1690, and her body rests today beneath the altar of the chapel there, still visited by pilgrims from across the world.
The devotion to the Sacred Heart she once struggled even to have believed by her own sisters has become one of the most widely practiced devotions in the entire Catholic Church.

This occurred in the centuries since her canonization—proof that a private mystical experience, however doubted and however delicate its bearer, can, once patiently and properly discerned, shape the prayer life of millions who never knew her name.
